# Notes on 1 Chronicles 26 for a verse-by-verse commentary

**What I found:** The sources I could read were older commentaries (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit, Keil & Delitzsch, Clarke, Matthew Henry, JFB), Guzik (Enduring Word), Precept Austin, Bible Hub, the Garner-Howes Baptist commentary, Kingcomments and the NET text. I found nothing on this chapter from the Lutheran, Methodist, Catholic, Orthodox or prosperity/word-of-faith sites, and no real disagreement between Protestant traditions. I couldn't open the Keil & Delitzsch page in full, so its notes below come from search snippets only.

## vv. 1–19: The gatekeepers

**v. 1**
- Guzik: gatekeepers had the responsibility for security, both in a practical and spiritual sense, letting in only those ready to worship. He also quotes Selman's view that their job was to show ordinary people the "practical limits of holiness," since entering the sanctuary unlawfully meant death. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-26/
- "Asaph" here is not the famous singer. Guzik, quoting Trapp, says he is another Asaph, called also Ebiasaph. The Pulpit Commentary agrees: Ebiasaph was a Korahite, while the singer Asaph was a Gershonite. Pulpit also says Meshelemiah is the same man called Shelemiah (v. 14) and Shallum (9:19). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-26.html
- Clarke: there were four classes of gatekeepers, one for each of the four temple gates. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-chronicles-26.html

**vv. 2–3**
- Pulpit: these verses list Shelemiah's seven sons. The firstborn, Zechariah, is also named in 1 Chr 9:21. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-26.html

**vv. 4–5 ("God had blessed Obed-edom")**
- Pulpit links "God blessed him" to 1 Chr 13:14 and 2 Sam 6:11, where God blessed Obed-edom's house while the ark stayed there. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-26.html
- Clarke quotes a comment that the blessing came because of the ark of the Lord which was in his house. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-chronicles-26.html
- Precept Austin: Obed-edom had sheltered the ark, after the death of Uzza (1Ch 13:14) and God had not forgotten his faithfulness. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-26-commentary
- Kingcomments: God honoured him with eight sons and gave his family a gate and the storehouse to look after. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/1-chronicles-26.html
- **Is this the same Obed-edom?** Precept Austin, citing Unger, calls him "the Gittite" from the Levite town of Gath-rimmon, not the Philistine city of Gath. It also notes some scholars believe that Obed-edom the gatekeeper was a man other than the one referred to above. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-26-commentary
- Keil & Delitzsch: this passage shows Obed-edom was a Korahite, from the Kohathite family. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-chronicles-26.html

**vv. 6–7**
- Guzik: Shemaiah's sons rose to high positions because they were men of great ability. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-26/
- Clarke: the gatekeepers were a military guard for the gates, not just doorkeepers. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-chronicles-26.html
- A Hebrew wording problem in v. 7: Ellicott says the Hebrew reads "his brethren" and seems to be missing an "and," so he reads it as "and his brethren… Elihu and Semachiah." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-26.html. Pulpit agrees the brethren were probably Elihu and Semachiah. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-26.html

**v. 8**
- Pulpit: the Hebrew is singular, which seems meant to give the description "strong, capable" to every single descendant of Obed-edom. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-26.html

**v. 9**
- Pulpit: the return to Meshelemiah puts his 18 next to Obed-edom's 62, making 80 Korahite gatekeepers. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-26.html

**vv. 10–11 (Shimri made "first")**
- Pulpit thinks the Hebrew more likely means "there was not a firstborn": the firstborn's family line had died out. It argues that if a firstborn had really been passed over, the text would have explained why. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-26.html
- Pulpit: Hosah's 13 bring the total to 93. — same URL

**v. 12**
- Guzik: the Chronicler shows that the gatekeepers' practical work was esteemed by God as just as valuable as the "spiritual" work. He quotes Selman that all tasks have value in the eyes of God. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-26/
- Keil & Delitzsch: the 93 named men are the heads over the 4,000 gatekeepers of 1 Chr 23:5. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-chronicles-26.html
- **Number differences.** Pulpit notes that the 93 here doesn't match the 212 of 1 Chr 9:22. It concludes numbers changed over time and finds no special ground for doubting the accuracy of the numbers. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-26.html

**v. 13 (casting lots)**
- Clarke: no captain was allowed to choose his gate; each was assigned by lot. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-chronicles-26.html
- Guzik: David let the LORD decide and did not let prestige or position count. He quotes Morgan that the church today seeks the Spirit's guidance instead of lots, but privilege should still carry no weight. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-26/
- Bible Hub links this to Proverbs 16:33 and says it avoided favouritism. — https://biblehub.com/1_chronicles/26.htm
- Kingcomments: the lot meant the LORD himself made the choice, without favouritism. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/1-chronicles-26.html

**v. 14 (Zechariah, "a wise counselor")**
- A Pulpit homily (Clarkson) uses the phrase to teach about the value of wise counsel in the church and the world. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-26.html
- ESV Study Bible (via Precept Austin): the east gate carried the most responsibility, because it led straight to the temple entrance. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-26-commentary

**v. 15 (the "storehouse," Hebrew *Asuppim*)**
- Gill: the word means "gathering." Some took it as a council house for the elders; Gill prefers a treasure house. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-chronicles-26.html
- Pulpit: probably a building for keeping sacred property safe, south of the temple. It also notes the Latin Vulgate took it as a council of elders. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-26.html

**v. 16**
- Pulpit: "Shuppim" makes no sense as a name here and is widely seen as a copying error that repeats the end of "Asuppim." Pulpit also discusses the Shallecheth Gate and its possible link to today's Bab Silsileh. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-26.html
- Gill notes that Shuppim is not mentioned anywhere earlier. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-chronicles-26.html

**vv. 17–18 (Parbar, "the court")**
- Clarke: the east gate had six guards because more people used it. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-chronicles-26.html
- Keil & Delitzsch count the posts and get 24 guard stations staffed every day. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-chronicles-26.html
- Pulpit: "Parbar" seems closest in meaning to "suburb," but what this Parbar really was is not yet ascertained. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-26.html
- Gill follows Lightfoot that Parbar means "suburbs," a western gate leading out to them. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-chronicles-26.html
- Garner-Howes (Baptist): Parbar was the area west of the temple, next to it. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-chronicles-26.html

**v. 19**
- Keil & Delitzsch confirm the gatekeepers were Korahites and Merarites. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-chronicles-26.html

## vv. 20–28: The treasurers

**v. 20 (a well-known text problem: "Ahijah" or "their fellow Levites")**
- Ellicott: the Hebrew is a strange beginning, since only Levites have been discussed so far. He follows the Greek Old Testament (LXX) and reads And the Levites their brethren were over the treasures. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-26.html
- Pulpit: no meaning can be got from "Ahijah" where it stands, and the LXX correction may be safely accepted. — https://biblehub.com/1_chronicles/26-20.htm. This is why the BSB, NIV and NET read "their fellow Levites" (NET: https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=1Ch+25:1--26:32&mode=text).
- Gill (on Bible Hub) keeps "Ahijah" as an actual official who at first had charge of both treasuries. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/26-20.htm
- ESV Study Bible (via Precept Austin): one treasury held regular tithes and offerings, the other the dedicated gifts, such as spoils of war. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-26-commentary
- Matthew Henry sees these treasures as a picture of the plenty in the Father's house and the unsearchable riches of Christ. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/26-20.htm
- The Douay-Rheims (Catholic) translation reads "Achias… and the holy vessels." This is a difference of wording only; I found no Catholic commentary on it. — https://biblehub.com/1_chronicles/26-20.htm

**vv. 21–22**
- Ellicott reads the two verses as one sentence: the Gershonite sons of Jehieli (Zetham and Joel) were over the treasures. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-26.html
- Pulpit: Ladan is the same person called Libni elsewhere. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-26.html

**v. 23**
- Pulpit: the four clans stand together for Kohath. Izharites and Hebronites reappear in vv. 29–31. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-26.html

**v. 24**
- Ellicott: the office of comptroller-in-chief of the treasures was hereditary in the house of this Amramite. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-26.html
- Garner-Howes points out these treasurers descended from Moses. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-chronicles-26.html

**v. 25**
- Gill reads the names as successive generations from Eliezer. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-chronicles-26.html
- Pulpit thinks they were more probably four brothers, all sons of Rehabiah, but says this can't be stated for certain. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-26.html

**vv. 26–27**
- Gill: the spoils were set aside for when the temple was built, to repair it and provide sacrifices. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-chronicles-26.html
- Pulpit points to 2 Sam 8:10–12 for these war proceeds. A Pulpit homily (Clarkson) teaches that all treasure is the Lord's and that looking after church money is an honourable stewardship. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-26.html
- Garner-Howes: Shelomith guarded spoils that had built up over several generations. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-chronicles-26.html

**v. 28**
- Pulpit: oddly, these gifts by Samuel, Saul, Abner and Joab aren't mentioned anywhere else in the history. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-26.html
- Gill: Shelomith oversaw all the treasuries, not just one part. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-chronicles-26.html

## vv. 29–32: Officials and judges

**v. 29**
- Keil & Delitzsch: the "outside duties" meant serving as scribes and judges (the 6,000 of 1 Chr 23:4). They reject Bertheau's view that it meant collecting temple dues. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-chronicles-26.html
- Pulpit: "officers" is better translated "scribes." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-26.html
- Matthew Henry: The magistracy is an ordinance of God for the good of the church as truly as the ministry is. The Levites knew the law better than tribal elders did. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_026.cfm
- A Pulpit homily (Clarkson): since Israel was a theocracy, Levites held civil office, and believers today may rightly serve the state. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-26.html
- Bible Hub: David met the command in Deuteronomy 16:18 to have judges in every town. — https://biblehub.com/1_chronicles/26.htm

**v. 30**
- Pulpit: "all the business of the LORD" probably shows that ordinary civil duties also counted as the Lord's work. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-26.html
- Guzik: Levites served as officials and judges across the kingdom, covering both spiritual matters and the king's affairs. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-26/

**v. 31**
- Keil & Delitzsch read the verse as a side-note explaining David's choice. Jazer was a Levite city in Gad, assigned to the Merarites. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-chronicles-26.html
- Matthew Henry: the fortieth year was David's last. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/26-29.html

**v. 32 (why 2,700 east but 1,700 west?)**
- Matthew Henry: either the remote eastern tribes lacked judges, or, living on the borders, they were most at risk from idolatry. The frontiers must be well guarded. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_026.cfm
- Keil & Delitzsch: the totals reach only 4,400 of the 6,000, so the list is probably incomplete. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-chronicles-26.html
- Pulpit: here "heads" must mean heads of households, not heads of whole clans. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-26.html
- Guzik quotes Payne that the statistic hints at how important Gilead was. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/1-chronicles/1-chronicles-26.cfm

## Devotional readings (traditional, not disputed)
- Guzik, Spurgeon-style: the "temple of the heart" needs a doorkeeper for the thoughts that come and go. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-26/
- Kingcomments: believers should be gatekeepers of their own hearts. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/1-chronicles-26.html
